query: Two Cups on the Bench {On the bench by the humming pear there's a flask and two chipped cups, and a note in Old Maud's hand. "One for you, dearie, one for whoever comes."|The flask on the bench again, still warm, still with two cups. Maud is never here when you are; the tea always is.|The flask, the cups, the note. You've started leaving the cups washed, and Maud has started leaving a biscuit.} {The silver bees are busy.|The ferns are glowing even in daylight.|{season == "winter": Frost on the bench, steam from the flask.|Blossom has settled in one of the cups.}} Sit and drink the tea {The tea tastes of honey and something green. You sit till the cup is cold and feel mended in some small, specific way.|You drink your cup and leave the second for whoever comes. Nobody does, but the pear hums as if someone had.|You drink, eat the biscuit, and wash both cups at the spring. The garden seems to approve of good manners.} Weed the beds for her {You leave the tea and weed the beds by the wall until your knees are green and your back is stiff. Maud will know, somehow.|You pull weeds that pull back, and one of them draws blood. The ferns lean away from the worst of them, gratefully.|You weed the far beds until your palms blister, and find a trowel Maud must have lost years ago. You leave it on the bench, by the cups.}

results.title: Weeding, Dearie
results.excerpt:
Weeding, Dearie
Old Maud looks at you for a long moment over her spectacles, the way she looks at a plant that's been kept in the wrong window. "You've a cold look about you, dearie," she says, and holds out a trowel. "Weeds don't pull themselves. Neither does the rest."
